cards.title: Adapt Ritual and Status Instead of Fighting Cultural Beliefs
cards.summary: Lion Guardians changed a Maasai rite of passage from killing lions to saving them by honoring underlying desires.
cards.use_when: Adapting a brand, product or category to sensitive cultural or identity-driven customer behaviors.

cards.title: Segment by Affiliation vs Dominion Worldview
cards.summary: Some buyers measure status by who trusts them; others by who has power—design messages for the metric they use.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative, influencer briefs or loyalty messaging for distinct buyer segments.

cards.title: Engineer a Standing Ovation: Seed a Small Number of Status Leaders
cards.summary: A few respected insiders can trigger a cascade of public adoption, but only where trust and belonging are strong.
cards.use_when: Planning product launches, review/social-proof seeding, or community engagement campaigns.

cards.title: Define the 'Us' Explicitly in Marketing Statements
cards.summary: When saying 'people like us do things like this,' a specific 'us' is required—otherwise the statement means nothing.
cards.use_when: Writing brand manifestos, community guidelines, or acquisition copy that invokes an in-group.

cards.title: Use the Roots and Shoots Metaphor to Plan Brand Growth
cards.summary: Deep roots in a niche's dreams and desires let the brand grow into a beacon that crowds out commodity competitors.
cards.use_when: Planning long-term brand differentiation and category dominance instead of rapid commodity launches.

cards.title: Position Just Ahead of Today—But Not Too Far
cards.summary: Meaningful change sits one step ahead of current culture; leap too far and the tribe will not follow.
cards.use_when: Designing product aesthetics, campaign concepts or brand refresh that must read as fresh but still familiar.

cards.title: Build a Peer-Powered Ratchet Like Slack
cards.summary: Products used together by teams gain a selfish reason for existing users to convert coworkers—driving viral pattern interrupts.
cards.use_when: Designing referral mechanics, collaboration features, subscription plans for teams, or buyer-side network effects.

cards.title: Interpret Famous Cases Without Copying Tactics Blindly
cards.summary: The tactic in a famous success (gala, format, campaign) is rarely the actual secret—the peer pressure and context is.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to replicate a well-known competitor's marketing format or campaign structure.

cards.title: Write a five-part business plan for a store launch or reposition
cards.summary: Replace the boilerplate business plan with five sections—Truth, Assertions, Alternatives, People, Money—so a store's direction and assumptions are testable before you spend on inventory and ads.
cards.use_when: Planning a new product line, store launch, brand repositioning or annual plan and you need an honest internal document rather than an investor compliance exercise.

cards.title: Choose dominion or affiliation status signals for your customers
cards.summary: Customers read your store through either a vertical dominance lens (winners/losers) or a horizontal affiliation lens (insiders/outsiders), and the customer's worldview, not yours, determines which works.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand voice, creative direction and community mechanics for a store—especially when you must pick between aggressive competitive positioning and belonging-based positioning.

cards.title: Use semiotics so your store reminds buyers of the right thing
cards.summary: Shoppers scan rather than study, asking 'what does this remind me of?', so logos, page styling, photography and packaging should be engineered to trigger the associations you want before anyone reads your copy.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a storefront, PDP photography, packaging, email design or ad creative where first-impression trust is at stake.

cards.title: Fly a specific flag instead of claiming no brand identity
cards.summary: A brand is the customer's shorthand for what you promise, and the smallest viable market means the right flag is a narrow, deliberate choice—not a message broad enough for everyone.
cards.use_when: Running brand positioning work, naming a store, writing taglines or choosing the aesthetic that determines who self-selects into your customer base.

cards.title: Aim new products at neophiliacs first, not the whole market
cards.summary: Roughly the left tail of the distribution actively seeks novelty, and the source argues that spending time or money trying to convert satisfied customers is wasted until the idea reaches them peer-to-peer.
cards.use_when: Deciding who to seed a new product, launch, bundle or category with first, and how to allocate launch marketing budget.

cards.title: Earn enrollment instead of buying attention
cards.summary: Enrollment is voluntary education—customers eagerly lending attention because they expect insight or forward motion—and the source frames it as the consensual first step of a mutual journey.
cards.use_when: Designing launch content, email opt-ins, community or loyalty programs, and deciding what you offer in exchange for a shopper's attention.

cards.title: Identify and multiply overinvest in your superusers
cards.summary: Everyone has a publishing platform now, but not everyone uses it, so the profitable move is to watch who actually advocates for you and give those people something worth talking about.
cards.use_when: Designing reviewer, UGC, refer-a-friend, ambassador or loyalty programs and deciding where to concentrate service and perks.

cards.title: Separate goal, strategy and tactics before running campaigns
cards.summary: A goal is the change you seek, strategy is the durable way you invest toward it, and tactics are the hundreds of replaceable steps—confusing the three makes stores abandon working strategies when a tactic underperforms.
cards.use_when: Setting annual marketing direction, deciding whether to drop a channel, or aligning a team on what counts as failure.

cards.title: Decide whether to buy ads at all—and which kind
cards.summary: Online advertising is simultaneously the most precise, instant and measurable channel ever and the most ignored, so the source says buy direct only when you can measure every step, and buy brand only if you can be patient and consistent.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget between paid acquisition and brand-building, or judging whether a paid channel should be scaled or killed.

cards.title: Build frequency before judging a message dead
cards.summary: People trust what they rehearse, so campaigns that seem stale to you may only just be landing with your market—quitting during the dip forfeits the trust the repetition was building.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to refresh ad creative, retire a tagline, change a packaging story or abandon a channel that hasn't produced results yet.

cards.title: Make your store the thing people search for by name
cards.summary: Generic search rankings can't support every business, so the durable path is building a product or service people care enough to look up specifically—then being what they find when they type your name.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in generic-term SEO, brand-name search, or marketplace and paid placement for a store with limited budget.

cards.title: Price as positioning signal, not just revenue math
cards.summary: Price tells a story about who you are for, and the margin it creates funds the outbound marketing that gets you noticed—so the number is a positioning decision before it's a spreadsheet cell.
cards.use_when: Setting price points, launching a premium or value line, or deciding whether to compete on cheapest price.

cards.title: Handle price discrimination with story, not mechanics
cards.summary: The price tag itself was an innovation built on treating buyers equally, and the source says the hard part of variable or dynamic pricing today is the storytelling, not the implementation.
cards.use_when: Planning discounts, member pricing, dynamic pricing, flash sales, Kickstarter-style tiers or loyalty pricing—and anticipating customer reaction.

cards.title: Storytelling Your Price (and Tiers) Instead of Racing to Cheapest
cards.summary: Price is a story to narrate on your PDP and offers, not a race to the bottom; design tiers, scarcity and discounts with a deliberate narrative.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending product pricing, launching a discount or dynamic-pricing policy, or building a tiered offer on a product page.

cards.title: Free Ideas, Paid Souvenirs: Structuring Your Giveaway-to-Purchase Ladder
cards.summary: Give away ideas and content for free to build reach and permission, then monetize the expensive tangible 'souvenir' expressions of those ideas.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to give away free (content, guides, tools, samples) versus what to charge for in your product line and funnel.

cards.title: High Price as a Trust-Building Device (Not a Trust Killer)
cards.summary: Counterintuitively, large or risky purchases can manufacture trust through cognitive dissonance, so lowering price is not the way to earn confidence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to discount to overcome buyer hesitation on a high-consideration item, membership or premium service.

cards.title: Who Is This Change For: Segmenting by Status, Not Just Demographics
cards.summary: Before changing price, tipping, packaging or offer structure, decide explicitly who the change excludes and how the customer's status story changes.
cards.use_when: Rolling out a pricing, packaging, service-model or policy change that will affect existing customers, and choosing which customers you are willing to lose.

cards.title: Earn Permission Before You Buy Attention: The Owned-List Rule
cards.summary: Build an owned permission asset (people who would miss you if you stopped) before leaning on paid ads or platform followers.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest acquisition effort and how to treat email/SMS lists, subscriptions and follower bases.

cards.title: Generosity at the Top of the Funnel: Launch to Neophiliacs Without Selling
cards.summary: Reach the small group of novelty-seeking early adopters with real news and generosity, not a hard pitch, and let them spread the word.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch, community seeding or influencer campaign for a brand-new offer with no existing audience.

cards.title: Remarkability Is Decided by Users, So Build Talkability Into the Product
cards.summary: You cannot declare your store remarkable; users decide, and the best reason they share is because sharing reflects well on them.
cards.use_when: Designing product, packaging, service or post-purchase moments intended to generate word-of-mouth.

cards.title: Designing Evangelism Into the Offer: Giving Customers a Reason to Tell Others
cards.summary: People will not spread your word because it matters to you; design the offer so sharing advances the customer's own goals.
cards.use_when: Building referral mechanics, shareable content, community features or product designs meant to generate peer-to-peer spread.

cards.title: Fixing a Leaky Funnel: Six Levers for Store Conversion
cards.summary: Treat your funnel as leaky and work six specific levers: right people, aligned promise, fewer steps, support, tension, and a megaphone.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where a store or landing-page funnel loses buyers and deciding what to change next.

cards.title: Funnel Math with LTV: When Ads Pay and When to Fix the Funnel First
cards.summary: Do the staged arithmetic from first click to loyal customer, compare acquisition cost with customer lifetime value, and refuse to buy ads you can't trace.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad budgets and channels, diagnosing an unprofitable paid campaign, or setting the target CAC for a store.

cards.title: Why Magical Self-Running Funnels Are Rare — Build the Post-Click Cohort
cards.summary: Most funnels cannot be passive profit machines; use ads to prime the pump, then build trust, trial, and a cohort that stays.
cards.use_when: Evaluating the promise of an automated or passive acquisition system, and deciding how much effort to put after the first click.

cards.title: Trust Through Action: What You Do Outweighs What You Say
cards.summary: In a low-trust environment, buyers remember what you did long after they forget what you said, so invest in service actions, not messaging.
cards.use_when: Handling refunds, defective products, data problems, fulfillment errors or any moment when the store's behavior is visible to a customer.

cards.title: Famous to the Smallest Viable Audience, Not the Biggest Number
cards.summary: Aim to be known to a small, right-sized tribe (the source's 'fifteen hundred to three thousand people') rather than maximizing follower counts.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to concentrate brand and PR effort, and how to measure community reach versus raw audience size.

cards.title: The Chasm: Why Early Buyers Won't Carry You to the Mass Market
cards.summary: Early adopters want new and risky while the mass market wants safe and proven, so plan a bridge instead of assuming the first group will spread the word.
cards.use_when: Planning category entry, product-market expansion or launch sequencing when early-adopter traction has not converted into mainstream sales.

cards.title: Crossing the Local Chasm: Yo-Yos, Facebook and Village Water
cards.summary: Crossing doesn't require a global leap — a well-seeded local adoption with low entry cost and identity can change everything.
cards.use_when: Seeding a product in a specific community, campus, niche or region before attempting broader rollout.

cards.title: Divide the Market into Short Heads: Escaping the Long-Tail Trap
cards.summary: Being one obscure item on an infinite shelf rarely pays; create the definitive hit for a defined niche so you become its short head.
cards.use_when: Choosing product selection strategy, niche assortment breadth, or deciding whether to compete as a tiny seller on a giant marketplace.

cards.title: Learning From HugDug's Failure: Trial Without Whales and Tension Dies
cards.summary: A cautionary case from the source: thousands of pages were built but almost no 'whales' promoted them, because tension and status incentives were missing.
cards.use_when: Designing a user-generated, community, referral or affiliate program and setting realistic time-to-traction expectations.

cards.title: Casey Neistat's Funnel Numbers: Reading Stage Conversions Realistically
cards.summary: A worked example of a large-permission-asset funnel: roughly 1,000,000 views to 18,000 to 1,000 to 5, showing steep attrition at each step.
cards.use_when: Setting realistic expectations for a content-to-conversion funnel and deciding which stage to improve.

cards.title: Make early product adoption visible and easy to discuss
cards.summary: Use recognizable product artifacts and observable benefits to help satisfied early buyers introduce a product to their peers.
cards.use_when: Launching an unfamiliar product or replenishment habit where mainstream shoppers need peer reassurance.

cards.title: Write a founder-to-customer narrative using self, us and now
cards.summary: Connect a credible founder experience to a shared customer need and an honest next action.
cards.use_when: Writing an About page, launch email or founder-led product video.

cards.title: Build customer community around shared practices
cards.summary: Give buyers meaningful ways to connect around a product interest instead of treating a community solely as a sales audience.
cards.use_when: Designing a brand community for products connected to a shared hobby, practice or identity.

cards.title: Maintain the community after launch excitement fades
cards.summary: Treat ongoing customer connection as recurring work rather than a campaign that sustains itself.
cards.use_when: Planning ownership and cadence for a store community, loyalty program or customer education series.

cards.title: Give cautious shoppers repeated consistent evidence
cards.summary: Allow mainstream buyers time and multiple useful encounters to evaluate an unfamiliar brand.
cards.use_when: A product attracts early adopters but struggles to reach more cautious shoppers.

cards.title: Position an upgrade around a meaningful change in identity or outcome
cards.summary: Explain why a buyer with a working alternative would care about a genuinely different product.
cards.use_when: Launching a premium replacement or upgrade in a mature product category.

cards.title: Ship a credible brand experience and improve from customer response
cards.summary: Use a usable launch to learn rather than delaying indefinitely for aesthetic perfection.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page or brand launch is ready for a limited initial release.

cards.title: Audit brand promises for value the customer actually receives
cards.summary: Assess persuasion by the delivered customer experience, not only the immediate sale.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a campaign or product-page promise that could raise short-term conversion while harming trust.

cards.title: Run the Comfort Trap check on product and name candidates
cards.summary: Judge shortlisted product, bundle or brand-name ideas by how polarizing they are, because full-consensus ideas tend to be invisible while mixed reactions signal energy.
cards.use_when: Choosing which new product, bundle concept, or brand name to take forward from a shortlist of candidates.

cards.title: Suspend evaluation to keep ideas alive during ideation
cards.summary: Delay judging new ideas so the team stays in divergent, problem-solving mode instead of shutting down candidates early.
cards.use_when: Running a brainstorm for a product launch, seasonal campaign, bundle concept or PDP angle where early criticism keeps killing options.

cards.title: Use approximate thinking to collect half-formed ideas
cards.summary: Ask contributors to stop at the 'approximate' stage — between absurd and safe — so ideas are captured before being fully baked or discarded.
cards.use_when: Designing a team or customer ideation session for new products, offers, campaigns or merchandising concepts.

cards.title: Name as Highest-Frequency Brand Lever
cards.summary: Treat the brand name as the highest-frequency, longest-lived asset you own, and judge it by whether it creates cumulative strategic advantage rather than by comfort.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much effort and budget to put into naming an ecommerce brand, product line or sub-brand before launch instead of accepting a Friday-afternoon placeholder name.

cards.title: Run a Category Audit Before Naming Anything
cards.summary: Map every existing name in the category first so you can define where you will not go, then mine product, consumer need and the ultimate benefit before generating any names.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, sub-brand or storefront when the category is full of descriptive names (fiber, mop, natural, fresh) and you need a defensible direction rather than a list of words.

cards.title: Name the Ultimate Benefit, Not the Product Category
cards.summary: Move the brand away from describing the category and toward the emotional or functional endpoint the buyer actually wants.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP hero copy, naming a new SKU, or repositioning a supplement, food or personal-care product where every competitor's label says the same category word.

cards.title: Quantity Leads to Quality: Generate Roughly 2,000 Names
cards.summary: Commit to large-volume generation with deliberate permission to produce bad ideas, because the source treats a 50-100 name list as the point where teams wrongly stop.
cards.use_when: Running any divergent naming, campaign or creative sprint for a store, SKU or ad concept and tempted to converge after the first hundred ideas.

cards.title: Replace Brainstorming With Small Teams and Shifting Briefs
cards.summary: Abandon group brainstorming; run two-person teams on deliberately different briefs so the candidate pool contains genuinely distinct naming directions.
cards.use_when: Structuring an internal or agency naming/creative sprint for a new brand, SKU or campaign and deciding how many people should work on it and with what information.

cards.title: Systematic Treasure-Hunt Databases for Naming
cards.summary: Mine enriched reference databases — roots, mythologies, the periodic table, plus your own cross-category archive — instead of waiting for inspiration.
cards.use_when: Filling the candidate pool for a new brand or product name when the obvious descriptive options are taken or legally blocked.

cards.title: Run a 20-Minute Personal Naming Session
cards.summary: Use a repeatable solo routine — free-associate on paper, ask AI for context rather than names, then chase promising directions into actual candidates.
cards.use_when: Sitting down to generate names or headline options yourself for a product, bundle or campaign and needing to get into flow quickly.

cards.title: Separate Divergence From Evaluation and Reframe Rejections
cards.summary: Protect the creative phase by replacing immediate rejection with problem-posing language, and delay real evaluation until later cycles.
cards.use_when: Reviewing creative submissions from staff or agencies — naming options, ad concepts, PDP concepts — and catching yourself about to kill an idea in the room.

cards.title: The Comfort Trap: Polarizing Names Carry Energy
cards.summary: Judge an idea by whether it sits in a high-energy tension zone or the invisible consensus zone, and treat strong internal polarization as a signal rather than a defect.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a safe, easily-approved brand name, campaign concept or offer angle and a polarizing one that some of your team dislikes.

cards.title: Present Names in Context, Not as a Spreadsheet
cards.summary: Show naming candidates inside realistic artifacts — press headlines, sponsored placements, product mock-ups — so decision-makers can feel how the name performs.
cards.use_when: Presenting name or brand options to founders, retailers or internal stakeholders who rarely make creative decisions and are choosing between unfamiliar candidates.

cards.title: Score Nameless Knowledge: Judging Names You Did Not Create
cards.summary: Evaluate names by expectedness relative to the owner, sound symbolism and familiarity-plus-surprise, rather than by personal taste.
cards.use_when: Choosing between shortlisted names for a brand, collection or product line and needing a consistent scoring rationale rather than gut preference.

cards.title: When to Rename and How to Launch It
cards.summary: The source's rule: names compound, so get it right early; when you do rename, lead with enthusiasm and a clear story rather than fear of losing equity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to change a store, product line or brand name that creates friction in search, spelling or customer recall, and planning the relaunch.

cards.title: Apply a Creative Curiosity Process
cards.summary: Operate naming and positioning work as a repeatable combination of category audit, product and consumer research, four strategy questions, then generation — not as one burst of inspiration.
cards.use_when: Setting up the brief for naming, positioning or a major PDP rewrite, or diagnosing why your creative output keeps landing in the invisible zone.

cards.title: Discipline, Not Talent: Managing Creative Contributors
cards.summary: Treat creativity as an acquired skill built through persistent process, and manage contributors by removing evaluation fear rather than by demanding brilliance.
cards.use_when: Founders or operators trying to scale creative output beyond themselves for naming, ad creative, PDP copy or content.

cards.title: Use an Inconvenient Outside Source to Force New Connections
cards.summary: Spend 30 minutes in unfamiliar material and deliberately look for transferable connections before finalizing creative work.
cards.use_when: A headline, PDP narrative, campaign angle or product story feels like generic category copy and you need a genuinely different perspective.

cards.title: Judging names is the scarce skill, not generating them
cards.summary: AI can mass-produce name candidates, so the durable advantage shifts to your ability to judge which names are right versus merely okay.
cards.use_when: When naming a new product, brand line, or store, or when you have a longlist of candidates and need to pick the one to launch with.

cards.title: Budget and scope for professional naming work
cards.summary: Name-development projects from an established naming firm typically run roughly $75k to $150k, with large corporate programs reaching about $200k, and usually include more than just the name.
cards.use_when: When planning budget, scope, or an in-house vs agency decision for a new brand, product line, or flagship SKU.

cards.title: Name launches usually include a post-launch tracking study
cards.summary: After delivering a name, naming firms often run small quantitative tracking research over 90-120 days to see how the name is landing with the market.
cards.use_when: When you have just launched or rebranded and want to know whether the new name is gaining traction before locking in packaging, listings and ad spend.

cards.title: Use 'approximate thinking' to unlock team creativity
cards.summary: Draw a line with bizarre/absurd/illegal ideas on one end and safe workable ideas on the other, put 'approximate thinking' in the middle, and explicitly give people permission to stop there instead of jumping straight to safe answers.
cards.use_when: When briefing your team or an agency on ad creative, product naming, landing-page concepts, or any ideation session where output has become predictable.

cards.title: Give AI the generation work, keep the judgment in-house
cards.summary: Integrating AI into a naming process took one firm about 16 months and shifted its edge from producing names to judging them against proprietary data.
cards.use_when: When deciding how far to automate naming, product-copy generation, or creative concepts, and what capability to keep human.

cards.title: The Daily 3: Cut to Three Needle-Movers
cards.summary: Each day pick only the top 3 tasks that move the store forward and say no to the other 97%.
cards.use_when: Weekly planning for a lean ecommerce team or solo operator overwhelmed by merchandising, marketing, and ops tasks.

cards.title: "Audience Comes Last": Build to Your Taste, Not Market Guessing
cards.summary: Ignore surveys and focus groups during the creative act; rely on personal intuition and taste, then test in market.
cards.use_when: Designing brand identity, packaging, creative direction, or new products where you're tempted to poll customers first.

cards.title: Let Weirdness Become the Brand's Authentic Edge
cards.summary: Digging into your own quirks and 'woo woo' interests produces authentic differentiation competitors don't copy.
cards.use_when: Positioning a store in a crowded category where every brand sounds and looks the same.

cards.title: Obsess Over the Craft, Not the Metrics
cards.summary: Betting maximum effort on the craft every time compounds exponentially, and obsession becomes contagious to an audience.
cards.use_when: Allocating effort between chasing metrics (views, follower counts) versus improving the actual product, photos, or content quality.

cards.title: Insanely Simple: Strip to One Idea
cards.summary: Relentlessly simplify products, UX, and messaging to one clear thing, on the Henry Ford principle that people don't know what they want.
cards.use_when: Simplifying a cluttered PDP, navigation, product line, or ad concept that has too many competing messages.

cards.title: Choose One Format on One Platform
cards.summary: Dabbling across platforms gets lost in the noise; obsessing over a single format on a single platform sets you apart.
cards.use_when: Deciding which organic channel to build for a store instead of posting thinly across X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Instagram.

cards.title: Go Deep, Not Wide: Shape the Company's Character
cards.summary: Iconic brands go deep rather than wide, and deliberately training through 'pain and suffering' refines a company's character.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to broaden a product line or deepen an existing category and internal standard of quality.

cards.title: Inject custom Liquid sections into a Shopify theme via Edit Code
cards.summary: Click path for creating a reusable custom section file in a Shopify theme by pasting external HTML/Liquid through the Edit Code interface.
cards.use_when: You need a custom PDP, landing page, or storefront section (founder block, ingredient panel, size chart) that Shopify's default page builder sections cannot produce, and want it reusable across templates.

cards.title: Assign a product to a custom page template
cards.summary: Click path for building a custom Shopify product template that hides default sections and populates your custom Liquid section with a specific product.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a hero or specialty product on a bespoke PDP layout, or building a landing page where you want your custom section to render that product's data.

cards.title: Make a product buyable with inventory set before launch
cards.summary: Ensuring a freshly added Shopify product can actually be added to cart by editing the product and setting available inventory.
cards.use_when: After adding a product through Products, Add product, before driving any traffic — you need to confirm the product is not showing as sold out or unavailable at checkout.
